name: Mundari (Retired)
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.quote: Acoustic cues such as intensity, duration, and fundamental frequency provide mixed results in identifying prominence within Mundari disyllables. However, the current study suggests that vowels are more dispersed and distinct in the second syllable compared to the first. Additionally, consonant duration in onset position is generally longer in the second syllable, except for voiced consonants and when the second syllable onset is preceded by a coda in the first syllable. Thus, there are indications of potential segmental distinctions between the first and second syllables of disyllables. This also manifests in an iambic pattern, where mid vowel quality and consonant duration serves as a cue. Consequently, prominence cued by consonant duration, and maximally contrastive mid vowels are more likely to occur in the second syllable of disyllabic words.

new_statements.rule_in_words: No agreed rule. The modern instrumental work finds no consistent acoustic word-level stress cue (duration marks utterance/phrase ends, intensity and F0 are inconsistent) and only a weak segmental tendency toward second-syllable (iambic) prominence in disyllables; the authors doubt Mundari even justifies a phonological-word level. The older impressionistic descriptions held by the project contradict one another: Nottrott 1882:6 and Hoffmann 1903:4 say mostly initial (Hoffmann: even when the final is checked, with a few lexical final-accent exceptions); Gumperz & Biligiri 1957:8-9 (via SPA 1979) say stress is nearly even with the last syllable slightly stronger and glottalized syllables strongest; Langendoen 1963:14-16 derives an alternating pattern with the penult de-accented when followed by exactly one consonant; Cook 1965:100 (via StressTyp2) says final if closed else penult; Sinha 1975:39 and Osada 2008 (via Horo & Anderson 2021 / Horo et al. 2023) say second syllable, trisyllables always second. This is the same conflict the catalog already records for mund1320.
new_statements.secondary_stress: None stated as a rule. Langendoen 1963:15 assigns an alternating (2)1..21 stress pattern within the word (secondary = level-2 accent on alternate vowels); Horo et al. 2023:81 report only a phonetic secondary intensity/F0 peak on the final syllable of tetra-/pentasyllables in sentence frames.
new_statements.exceptions: Hoffmann 1903:4: 'There are few exceptions to this rule. They must be learned by practice. I have so far not ascertained the reason of the accentuation of the last syllable in those words.' Nottrott 1882:6: infinitives and words ending in a diphthong take the antepenult. Langendoen 1963: Rule 21 (vowel neutralization) is dialect-limited and cuts across the Hasada/Naguri division; checked vowels may perturb the alternating pattern. Horo et al. 2025:148: results from only 4 of 10 speakers, 'premature to draw any broad conclusions'.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level is the object of every description, but Horo et al. 2023:81 show duration is anchored to the utterance edge (isolated words and sentence frames were both recorded) and 2025:137 conclude 'Mundari is among the Austroasiatic languages that does not offer justification for the level of phonological word'. Gumperz & Biligiri 1957 speak of 'single word utterances'. Hoffmann and Nottrott describe citation forms impressionistically.
new_statements.identity_note: mund1339 is not a language: it is Glottolog's bookkeeping placeholder for the retired ISO 639-3 code [muw] 'Mundari', split by ISO CR 2007-065 (effective 2008-02-18) into [unr] Mundari = Glottolog mund1320 and [unx] Munda = Glottolog mund1321. The split rests on census/ethnonym grounds only; Glottolog 5.3 itself keeps mund1321 in bookkeeping because Munda and Mundari 'are part of the same language (Cook 1965, Grierson 1906, Osada & Onishi 2012)', and Horo, Anderson & Gogoi 2025:137 say the two census entries 'are two variants of the same thing'. Every source examined describes Mundari (Kherwarian, North Munda; Khunti/Ranchi, Jharkhand; dialects Hasada', Naguri, Kera', Tamaria named but not linguistically distinguished). Mundari mund1320 is already in the catalog (record, classification conflict, src qs-tier-2026-09-12) quoting Hoffmann 1903:4, Cook 1965/66:100 and Horo & Anderson 2021:314, with Horo et al. 2023 as the instrumental line. A separate record for mund1339 would double-count one language under a retired code.

new_statements.quote: [p. 100] Multi-syllabic morphemes are combinations of CV and CVC syllables. These patterns are accompanied by stress in accordance with the following rule" Stress:"If the final syllable of a morpheme is closed(CVC), then the final syllable is accented; If the final syllable is open (CV),then the preceding,or penultimate syllable is accented." This rule applies to stress within morphemes. Stress patterns in words would take further investigation. In general, stress tends to remain with the primary roots, with the formative elements generally unstressed. [p. 286] Open syllables are CV, closed syllables are CVC, but zero onset is allowed. Final closed syllables are stressed, but elsewhere stress is on the penultimate syllable.

new_statements.relation_note: No catalog record exists for mund1339 (bookkeeping). Against the one existing statement (Horo, Anderson & Gogoi 2025: acoustic cues mixed, no consistent word-level prominence, segmental cues hint at second-syllable prominence in disyllables; reading unclear or contradictory), Cook gives a definite weight-sensitive placement rule (final if closed, else penult), i.e. a different TYPE of statement. It is only partly compatible with Horo et al.: for CVCVC disyllables both point to the second syllable, but for CVCV disyllables Cook puts stress on the first. It also differs from the other descriptions already held by the project for this language: Hoffmann 1903:4 (accent generally on the first sy…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Within the morpheme, stress falls on the final syllable if it is closed (CVC); if the final syllable is open (CV), stress falls on the penult. Cook states this as a morpheme-domain rule and says word-level stress patterns need further investigation; in words, stress tends to stay on the primary root and formative (suffixal) elements are generally unstressed. He also notes (p. 92) that the diphthongs /ai/, /au/ in open syllables 'are generally stressed'. No tone is posited; vowel length is described as non-contrastive (p. 44). There is no separate suprasegmental chapter; stress is treated inside phonotactics and summarized in both conclusions.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing on secondary stress; only the remark that formative elements are generally unstressed and roots keep the stress.
new_statements.exceptions: Domain caveat: the rule is stated for morphemes, 'Stress patterns in words would take further investigation'; diphthongs /ai/, /au/ in open syllables (final or non-final) 'are generally stressed' (p. 92), which can override the penult default; formatives generally unstressed.
new_statements.identity_note: mund1339 is the Glottolog bookkeeping entry for retired ISO [muw], split in 2008 (CR 2007-065, census/ethnonym grounds) into unr Mundari (= mund1320, the catalog language) and unx Munda (= mund1321, itself bookkeeping 'per Cook 1965' among others). Cook 1965 describes Mundari as a whole, naming two principal dialects, Hasada (SE Ranchi district around Sarwada, no phonemic aspiration) and Naguri (west of the Ranchi-Chaibasa road, aspiration phonemic, more Hindi/Sadari loans) (printed p. 4 = p. 12), and treats Ho as near enough to be a Mundari dialect; his fieldwork was in Singhbhum District 1953-1962 with Menas Orea of Buruma, one of Hoffmann's informants (Preface p. iv). Every statement here therefore belongs to mund1320 Mundari.

readall_conflicts: The sources for Mundari disagree on both placement and type. Cook 1965 (pp. 100, 286) states a weight-sensitive morpheme-level rule: final syllable stressed if closed (CVC), otherwise the penult, roots keeping stress and formatives unstressed. Hoffmann 1903:4 puts the accent generally on the first syllable of disyllables even when the last syllable is checked (which directly contradicts Cook's closed-final clause) and calls accentuation weak; Nottrott 1882 sect. 12 likewise says mostly first syllable. Gumperz & Biligiri 1957 (quoted in SPA 1979) say stress is predictable, fairly evenly distributed, the last syllable slightly more stressed but variable across tokens, with glottal-checked syllables more stressed. Langendoen 1963 derives an alternating pattern by rule. Horo, Anderson & Gogoi 2025 (and Horo, Gogoi & Anderson 2023) find no consistent acoustic cue to word-level prominence, with segmental cues weakly favouring the second syllable of disyllables. Cook agrees with the instrumental work only for CVCVC shapes; for CVCV shapes he sides with Hoffmann/Nottrott (first = penult). No two independent sources give the same rule, so the cross-source reading stays unclear or contradictory even though Cook's own statement, read alone, is weight-sensitive.

sources.citation: Horo, Luke, Pamir Gogoi & Gregory D. S. Anderson. 2023. Phonetic correlates of syllable prominence in Mundari. Proc. 2nd International Conference on Tone and Intonation (TAI 2023), Singapore, 78-82. doi 10.21437/TAI.2023-17.
sources.note: Instrumental (3 M + 3 F speakers): duration peaks on utterance-final syllables (not a word-level cue); intensity tends to peak on second syllables but is not a robust cue; F0 shows a gender split. Reviews the literature as disputed: Hoffmann trochaic/initial, Cook quasi-trochaic (initial and final), Sinha quasi-iambic (second syllable; trisyllables second, agreed by Osada 2008) (pp.78, 81).

sources.note: STRESS field quotes Gumperz & Biligiri 1957:8-9: 'In single word utterances length and stress are predictable and therefore not phonemic.. In words of more than one syllable stress is fairly evenly distributed. The last syllable is slightly more stressed than the rest, although occasionally in the same word, stress may be on the first syllable in one occurrence and on the second in another. Syllables ending in a phonetic [glottal stop] or a glottalized allophone of a stop are considerably more stressed than others.' (second-hand carrier of the 1957 primary).

sources.citation: Langendoen, D. Terence. 1963 [rekeyed 2010]. Mundari phonology. Unpublished ms., Munda Languages Project, University of Chicago (fieldwork summer 1962, Ranchi).
sources.note: Generative stress rules 17-21, pp.14-16: every vowel is accented, then Rule 18 removes accent from a penultimate vowel followed by exactly one consonant (penult keeps accent before CC or before no consonant: [baránda], [géléa]); Rule 19 assigns an alternating (2)1..21 pattern within the word; Rule 20 reduces stress on a final /a/ unless preceded by an unaccented vowel; dialect-limited Rule 21 neutralizes unaccented vowels before resonants. Author says checked vowels may perturb the pattern, 'I am not certain if so and how'.

sources.citation: Hoffmann, John. 1903. Mundari Grammar. Calcutta: Bengal Secretariat Press.
sources.note: p.4: 'In dissyllabic words the accent is generally on the first syllable even when the last syllable is checked.. There are few exceptions to this rule. They must be learned by practice.. accentuation is by far not as pronounced as in German or English. Barring some very short vowels, the accentuated has hardly more stress than the non-accentuated syllable.' (archive.org scanned; example words garbled).
